children.name: Brain Computer Interfaces
children.blurb: Brain computer interfaces are systems that read neural activity and translate it into signals a machine can act on, or that deliver stimulation back into nervous tissue.

children.name: Early Signals of Dementia
children.blurb: Early signals of dementia are subtle changes in memory, language, orientation and behaviour that appear years before a formal diagnosis, and the field studies them through cognitive testing, imaging, fluid biomarkers and digital behaviour traces.

children.name: Functional MRI Interpretation
children.blurb: Functional MRI interpretation covers the reading of blood oxygen level dependent signals to infer regional brain activity during tasks or at rest.

children.name: Cognitive Rehabilitation
children.blurb: Cognitive rehabilitation covers the therapies, exercises and assistive tools used to help people recover or compensate for changes in attention, memory, language and executive function after injury or illness.

sections.body: Neuroinformatics and the Brain covers the use of artificial intelligence on data recorded from the human nervous system, from electrode arrays to imaging scanners. In practice, the work is signal processing at scale: models learn to separate the neural signature of an intended movement from noise, to flag a scan region that differs from a healthy baseline, or to detect the electrical build up that precedes a seizure. Brain computer interfaces use this to turn cortical activity into control signals for cursors, robotic arms or speech prostheses, mostly in research settings and small clinical trials with implanted electrodes. Dementia work leans on speech, gait and imaging data to find patterns that precede a formal diagnosis. Functional MRI interpretation uses learned models to map activation and connectivity, and seizure prediction uses continuous EEG to estimate when a seizure is likely. Cognitive rehabilitation applies similar methods to track recovery and tailor exercises after injury or illness.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some parts of this field are genuinely working. Seizure detection from EEG is well established, and closed loop stimulation devices that respond to detected activity are approved for certain drug resistant epilepsies. Decoding intended movement for cursor control has improved steadily, and speech decoding from cortical signals has produced promising results in small studies. What is not solved is prediction in the everyday sense: warning a person hours ahead of a seizure remains unreliable, and false alarms are a real cost. Dementia signals are statistical associations, not diagnoses, and a model that flags risk in one cohort often performs worse in another because scanners, protocols and populations differ. Implanted interfaces degrade as scar tissue forms and require calibration, and most findings come from small samples that have not been replicated at scale. Functional MRI interpretation is also limited by what the signal actually measures, which is blood oxygenation rather than neural firing, so the maps are indirect.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages here follow the arc from signal to intervention. Brain Computer Interfaces is the entry point for decoding movement and intent, and it sets up the recording and calibration problems that recur elsewhere. Early Signals of Dementia takes the same pattern finding approach to subtle behavioural and imaging markers, where the honest question is what a flag means before symptoms appear. Functional MRI Interpretation sits underneath much of that work, explaining how activation and connectivity maps are produced and where their limits lie. Seizure Prediction is the most clinically mature thread, covering detection, forecasting and the false alarm problem. Cognitive Rehabilitation closes the loop, using tracked signals to guide recovery after injury or illness. A reader new to the area should start with Brain Computer Interfaces, then read Functional MRI Interpretation for the measurement background, and go to the remaining pages for the specific clinical problems.
